items.title: Patagonia's owner gave the company to the planet
items.claim: In September 2022, Yvon Chouinard announced he was transferring ownership of Patagonia. What was the structure?

options.text: An IPO on the New York Stock Exchange
All voting stock to the Patagonia Purpose Trust (climate-aligned governance); all non-voting stock (98%) to the Holdfast Collective, with future profits funding environmental causes
A sale to a private equity buyer

items.reveal:
Chouinard, his wife Malinda and their two children transferred Patagonia (valued around $3bn) using two vehicles: the Purpose Trust holds voting control to ensure mission alignment; the Holdfast Collective (a 501(c)(4) nonprofit) holds economic ownership and receives roughly $100m of annual profits to fund environmental work.

The structure required the family to pay $17.5m in gift tax. The company is a B Corp (certified since 2011) — the legal structure goes much further than B Corp certification alone.

B Lab's B Corp movement, launched in 2006, certifies firms meeting social and environmental performance standards.
items.why: Corporate ownership structures shape objectives. A trust-owned firm doesn't have to maximise shareholder returns — because its 'shareholders' are not the same as a public company's.

items.title: Quick ratio strips out the inventory you can't sell fast
items.claim: A retailer has current assets of £600,000 (including £400,000 inventory) and current liabilities of £300,000. What is the quick (acid-test) ratio?
items.reveal:
Quick ratio = (current assets - inventory) / current liabilities = (£600,000 - £400,000) / £300,000 = 0.67. Current ratio would be 2.0 — looking healthy. The acid-test reveals the firm could not cover short-term liabilities without selling stock.

The rule of thumb that quick ratio should exceed 1.0 is industry-dependent. Supermarkets routinely operate below 0.5 because they sell stock for cash before paying suppliers.
items.why: Two firms with identical current ratios can have very different real liquidity. Inventory turnover matters as much as the ratio number.

items.title: Herzberg's hygiene factors don't motivate
items.claim: Frederick Herzberg's 1959 'Motivation to Work' surveyed 200 engineers and accountants. What did he conclude about pay?

options.text: Pay is a 'hygiene factor' — low pay causes dissatisfaction but high pay does not produce sustained motivation. Motivators are achievement, recognition and the work itself
Pay had no effect either way
Only senior staff are motivated by pay

items.reveal:
Herzberg's two-factor theory splits job factors into hygiene (pay, conditions, supervision, policies) — whose absence causes dissatisfaction — and motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth) — which actively drive engagement.

Methodological critics note Herzberg used the 'critical incident' interview technique, in which people tend to attribute good experiences to themselves and bad ones to external factors. Replications using other methods get less crisp results.
items.why: Pay rises buy off dissatisfaction, not loyalty or effort. Most modern HR practice combines compensation (hygiene) with job design (motivators) — a direct legacy of Herzberg.
